title: Redwood Console + Rollouts: Shadow Evals dashboard (MVP demo)
summary: Redwood demoed early Console mockups/MVP for Shadow Evals: enabling per-route shadow sampling, selecting shadow targets (model/version/quant profile/prompt config), and viewing quality + performance comparisons without impacting primary responses. Customer focused on quota/cost controls, latency/SLO isolation, and how rollout gating works (what metrics are safe to gate on, and how to avoid false positives). Redwood walked through guardrails (capacity budgets, drop counters, kill switch), metric dimensions/cardinality, retention/redaction options, and how the shadow signals plug into canary/A-B policy rules.
topics: Shadow Traffic overview: mirrored requests, async execution, no user impact
Console UX: per-route configuration, shadow targets, sampling %, allowlists
Dashboard: win-rate / preference judge, format adherence, safety outcomes, latency & cost deltas
Quotas & budgets: per-account caps, per-route caps, drop/queue metrics, cost attribution
Rollout gating: policy thresholds, hold/rollback semantics, confidence & sample sizes
Security: retention, prompt/output redaction, restricted access, residency considerations
Operational controls: kill switch, backpressure, alerting on queue depth and shadow errors
questions: How do you enforce a hard budget so shadow evals can’t accidentally consume GPU capacity needed for primary traffic?
Will shadowing change batching/KV cache behavior in the primary path (even if responses aren’t blocked)?
Can we gate a rollout on judge win-rate, and how do you protect against judge drift / noise?
How is cost attributed for shadow runs (to the route, to the experiment, or to the account)?
What’s stored for judging—do prompts/outputs get logged, and what’s the default retention?
Can we disable shadowing instantly without a deploy, and what’s the verification step?
next_steps: Redwood to share a short write-up on quota/budget semantics (account cap vs per-route cap) and how drops are reported.
Customer to send their current rollout process and which metrics they consider acceptable for automated rollback.
Redwood to schedule a follow-up technical deep dive on data retention/redaction options with Security (Jordan) and SRE (Priya).
Redwood to enable a limited beta flag in customer sandbox for 1 route at 0.5% sampling, single shadow target, with latency/cost dashboards.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai - Transcript
Title: Redwood Console + Rollouts: Shadow Evals dashboard (MVP demo)
Date: 2025-11-12 10:03 AM PT
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Marissa Cole, Dylan Brooks, Chloe Martin, Paula Mendes (Redwood Inference); Anika Shah, Miguel Alvarez, Priya Raman, Jordan Kim (Finch Financial)

[00:00] Marissa Cole: Cool, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to show the early Shadow Evals experience in the Console, so you can react to the dashboard and also the controls—sampling, quotas, and how this hooks into rollouts.

[00:18] Anika Shah: Great. We saw the earlier email. We’re mainly trying to understand, like, what levers we have so this doesn’t become an unbounded cost center.

[00:27] Dylan Brooks: Yep, that’s exactly the right concern. And just upfront: shadow never blocks the primary response. It’s async, isolated, and it’s allowed to drop.

[00:38] Priya Raman: “Allowed to drop” is good. Like by design, it can just not run if things are hot?

[00:43] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. We treat it as best-effort. We track drop reasons, so you can see “budget exceeded” versus “queue full” versus “target unavailable.”

[00:54] Marissa Cole: I’ll share my screen.

[01:02] Marissa Cole: Okay, can you all see the Console? This is in our staging tenant so the numbers are fake-ish.

[01:08] Miguel Alvarez: Yep.

[01:10] Marissa Cole: Left nav—there’s a new section under Rollouts called “Shadow Evals.” MVP has two entry points: (1) enable shadowing per route, and (2) view results aggregated by route and target.

[01:24] Paula Mendes: And to be clear, this will be behind a beta feature flag initially.

[01:29] Marissa Cole: I’m clicking into Routes → /v1/chat/completions, this one is your “support-agent-prod” example. Here’s the “Shadow traffic” card.

[01:39] Marissa Cole: You can set sampling percent. In this mock it’s 1%. You can also set an allowlist—like only shadow requests from specific customer org IDs or internal users.

[01:49] Anika Shah: Does allowlist mean, like, our end customers? Or our accounts? We’re B2B2C.

[01:55] Chloe Martin: Good question. It maps to the identity we see in Redwood’s request metadata. For most customers it’s an “end_customer_id” or “tenant_id” they pass in headers. If you don’t pass one, it can’t be used for allowlist.

[02:10] Miguel Alvarez: So it’s not like you’re guessing from prompt content.

[02:12] Chloe Martin: No, it’s policy only. No prompt inspection for routing.

[02:17] Marissa Cole: Next is “Shadow targets.” In MVP you can add one or more targets. Each target is basically model + version, plus optional config profile—like quantization or prompt template.

[02:31] Marissa Cole: Here I have Target A: “llama-3.1-70b-instruct / build 2025-11-08 / int8-q.” Target B: “same model / fp16.”

[02:44] Miguel Alvarez: Wait, you can shadow quantization changes without changing the primary?

[02:47] Marissa Cole: Exactly. That’s one of the main use cases.

[02:52] Priya Raman: How are you doing the mirroring? Is it at the gateway?

[02:56] Dylan Brooks: It’s in the data plane after we’ve accepted the request and before the response is streamed out. We create a shadow job with the request payload, but it’s detached from the main execution. If shadow queue is overloaded, we just don’t enqueue.

[03:13] Priya Raman: So the gateway doesn’t fan out.

[03:15] Dylan Brooks: Correct. No gateway fan-out.

[03:18] Jordan Kim: From a security standpoint, that means the payload is duplicated somewhere. Where does it live?

[03:23] Chloe Martin: For the demo environment, we store a redacted payload blob for a limited retention to support judging and debugging. In prod you can configure retention and also set “no payload storage,” meaning we only keep derived metrics.

[03:39] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[03:41] Marissa Cole: Let me jump to the dashboard view. Shadow Evals → Overview. You can filter by route, time window, region, and primary model.

[03:54] Marissa Cole: Top line: “Shadow coverage”—how many primary requests were eligible, how many sampled, how many executed, and how many dropped.

[04:04] Anika Shah: That’s important. We’ve been burned where sampling says 1% but it’s actually 1% of retries too, or like… weird stuff.

[04:11] Dylan Brooks: Yeah. We define it as: “sampling decision is evaluated once per primary request_id.” Retries reuse request_id, so we don’t double-sample.

[04:22] Miguel Alvarez: Nice.

[04:24] Marissa Cole: Middle section is “Quality signals.” For MVP we have: (1) Format adherence, (2) Safety policy outcomes, (3) Similarity / diff metrics, and (4) LLM-as-judge preference.

[04:38] Miguel Alvarez: On “format adherence,” what’s that actually checking?

[04:41] Paula Mendes: It’s defined per route. If you have JSON schema or function call structure, we validate the shadow output matches the expected structure. For chat, it can be “valid tool call” or “valid JSON.” It’s not semantic correctness.

[04:55] Marissa Cole: In this chart: “Schema valid rate.” Primary is 99.2. Shadow target A is 99.1. Shadow target B is 98.4.

[05:08] Anika Shah: So you’d gate on that?

[05:10] Paula Mendes: Potentially, yes. That’s one of the safer ones because it’s deterministic.

[05:16] Marissa Cole: Next chart: “Judge win-rate.” This is the one people get excited about but also… you want guardrails.

[05:25] Miguel Alvarez: Yeah I’m skeptical. Judges can be noisy.

[05:28] Marissa Cole: Totally fair. In MVP we show confidence intervals and minimum sample sizes. And the rollout policy integration lets you say “don’t act until N comparisons.”

[05:40] Dylan Brooks: And we’re also planning to support “judge drift monitoring” where we periodically re-run a fixed calibration set.

[05:48] Miguel Alvarez: Is that in the product or like a process?

[05:51] Dylan Brooks: For beta, more process. GA we want it productized.

[05:58] Marissa Cole: Right side: “Performance deltas.” We break out end-to-end shadow latency, model latency, and estimated token cost. Importantly: this is shadow-side only. Primary latency is in the normal route dashboard.

[06:14] Priya Raman: Sorry, can we pause on that. You said it doesn’t affect primary latency. But you’re still doing some work to enqueue the shadow job. That overhead is…?

[06:24] Dylan Brooks: There is a small constant overhead, like microseconds to low milliseconds. But we budget it. If we can’t enqueue fast, we bail.

[06:34] Priya Raman: And the bigger concern is like shared GPU pressure affecting primary batching.

[06:40] Dylan Brooks: Yes. That’s why shadow has a separate capacity budget and rate limit. It’s not allowed to steal from primary pools. On hosted, we allocate a capped portion of GPU time. On dedicated, you can allocate a separate replica set or a fixed percent budget.

[06:58] Anika Shah: Okay, so quotas. This is the big one. Is quota measured in requests, tokens, dollars…?

[07:05] Marissa Cole: In the MVP mock, we show three knobs: max shadow RPS, max shadow tokens per minute, and a daily token cap. The idea is you can set both burst and sustained limits.

[07:16] Miguel Alvarez: That’s… a lot of knobs.

[07:18] Marissa Cole: Yeah. We’re still iterating. What we heard is folks want a simple “budget: $X/day” but under the hood we enforce tokens/RPS.

[07:28] Nadia Rahman: (not on the call, but I’ll mention) cost attribution is per route and per target. So you can see “this experiment cost you this many tokens.”

[07:35] Chloe Martin: To answer your earlier question: cost gets tagged with (route, primary_model, shadow_target). In billing you can roll it up to account and then drill down.

[07:46] Anika Shah: Can we make it “free” in the sense that it can’t exceed a fixed percent of our primary spend?

[07:54] Dylan Brooks: That’s on the roadmap. For beta we’ll do absolute caps. Percent-of-primary is trickier because primary spend isn’t known until after the fact, but we can approximate with moving averages.

[08:09] Miguel Alvarez: Okay. And if we have two shadow targets, does that double cost? Like does the sampled request go to both?

[08:16] Marissa Cole: Yes—if you configure two targets, one sampled primary request can fan out to both targets. So you would want to lower sampling or limit targets.

[08:25] Priya Raman: And concurrency? Because we had a case with Bedrock where background stuff piled up.

[08:31] Dylan Brooks: We cap concurrency per region and per account. And the queue is bounded. Once you hit the queue depth threshold, we start dropping new shadow jobs.

[08:41] Priya Raman: Do you alert on queue depth?

[08:43] Dylan Brooks: Yes. There’s an SRE dashboard panel and alert rules: queue depth, drop count, shadow error rate.

[08:52] Jordan Kim: You mentioned payload redaction. Is that like PII removal? How do you do that?

[08:58] Chloe Martin: Two layers: (1) header/body field allowlist—so we can exclude whole fields from being stored, and (2) text redaction filters for known patterns. For regulated customers we recommend not storing prompts/outputs at all, and just storing derived metrics.

[09:16] Jordan Kim: If you don’t store outputs, how do you do the judge?

[09:20] Chloe Martin: The judge can run in-line in the shadow pipeline and then we only store the judge score and explanation snippet, or even only the score. But the judge itself needs access to the output at runtime.

[09:32] Jordan Kim: And is the judge another model call? Like are you sending our data to OpenAI?

[09:37] Marissa Cole: By default, judge runs on Redwood-hosted judge models. We do not send to OpenAI unless you configure an external judge provider. For private deployments, you can run the judge inside your VPC.

[09:52] Anika Shah: What judge model do you use?

[09:55] Marissa Cole: For MVP we’ve been using a small-to-mid instruct model tuned for rubric scoring. We can share details under NDA. We also let you choose a judge from the catalog.

[10:09] Miguel Alvarez: How do you keep the judge from just preferring longer answers.

[10:12] Marissa Cole: Yeah, classic. We normalize length, we include explicit rubric constraints, and we calibrate on a prompt set. It’s not perfect, but it’s stable enough for regression detection.

[10:26] Paula Mendes: And in rollout policy, we recommend gating on judge only with multiple metrics. Like judge win-rate plus format adherence, plus safety outcomes.

[10:36] Marissa Cole: Let me show rollout gating. I’ll click Rollouts → Policies. Here’s a canary policy: “Model upgrade: llama-3.1-70b build 1108.”

[10:48] Marissa Cole: Under “Quality gates,” you can add a gate that references shadow metrics: “Hold canary if judge win-rate vs primary drops more than 3% for 15 minutes, min 500 samples.”

[11:03] Anika Shah: And what does “hold” do? Does it roll back automatically?

[11:07] Paula Mendes: There are three actions: notify only, hold, rollback. Hold stops traffic progression—like it freezes canary at the current percent. Rollback returns to baseline.

[11:20] Anika Shah: Okay.

[11:22] Priya Raman: What happens if shadow is unhealthy? Like queue is full so you’re not getting samples. Does it block the rollout?

[11:30] Paula Mendes: It depends on your policy. Default is: shadow health does not block rollout, because it’s optional. But you can add a guard like “require at least X shadow executed samples per window.”

[11:45] Miguel Alvarez: That’s nice. Otherwise people will stare at empty charts.

[11:49] Marissa Cole: On the right, we also show “shadow availability” as a status badge.

[11:56] Jordan Kim: Can you tie this to audit logs? Like who enabled shadowing on a route.

[12:02] Chloe Martin: Yes, route config changes are audited. Enabling shadowing is a control-plane change, so it’s logged with actor and time.

[12:11] Jordan Kim: Good.

[12:13] Anika Shah: I want to go back to “no impact.” We have strict p99. If this adds even 10ms, it’s a problem.

[12:22] Dylan Brooks: Understood. That’s why we built a perf canary that runs continuously and alerts if primary p99 shifts when shadow is enabled. Also, the enqueue path is extremely lightweight and can be disabled if it misbehaves.

[12:37] Priya Raman: Is there a kill switch.

[12:39] Dylan Brooks: Yes. Global kill switch and per-route disable. And it can be toggled without deploy.

[12:46] Priya Raman: Where is it toggled? Console or API?

[12:49] Chloe Martin: Both. Console for admins, and an admin API endpoint for automation.

[12:54] Priya Raman: And what’s the verification? Like after toggling, how do I know it’s off.

[13:01] Dylan Brooks: You look at “shadow_enqueued” dropping to zero and “shadow_disabled_by_killswitch” incrementing. Also queue depth should drain.

[13:11] Miguel Alvarez: So you emit a metric that says it was skipped because disabled.

[13:14] Dylan Brooks: Exactly.

[13:17] Marissa Cole: Quick note: we’re still refining naming, but yes.

[13:22] Anika Shah: On the dashboard, can we slice by customer tenant? Like if one tenant is weird and causes judge to fail.

[13:30] Marissa Cole: We’re not planning to expose raw tenant IDs as a dimension because cardinality and privacy. What we can do is allow filtering by allowlist group or by a limited set of labels you define.

[13:43] Chloe Martin: Basically you can define “cohort tags” with a small controlled vocabulary. We don’t want “unbounded user_id” in metrics.

[13:52] Anika Shah: Makes sense.

[13:54] Miguel Alvarez: What about prompt template version? That’s also high cardinality.

[13:59] Chloe Martin: Same story: you can tag a small number of prompt config versions. Or we bucket by “primary prompt config” vs “shadow prompt config.”

[14:09] Marissa Cole: In this mock, the filter is “prompt_config: v12/v13” but it’s actually a short name you choose.

[14:18] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[14:20] Marissa Cole: Let’s click into a specific target comparison view. Shadow Evals → Target A. Here you see side-by-side: primary vs shadow metrics.

[14:30] Marissa Cole: There’s also an “Examples” tab. For beta, this is restricted and heavily redacted. It shows a small sample of paired requests and outputs for debugging judge disagreements.

[14:43] Jordan Kim: That makes me nervous. Who can see examples.

[14:47] Marissa Cole: Admin-only by default, RBAC-controlled. And you can disable examples entirely.

[14:55] Jordan Kim: Default retention?

[14:57] Chloe Martin: Proposed default is 7 days for derived metrics, 0 days for raw payloads unless explicitly enabled. For beta we might keep a small sample for a short time with customer consent.

[15:11] Jordan Kim: Okay, we’d probably do 0 for payload.

[15:14] Anika Shah: Same.

[15:16] Miguel Alvarez: If no payload, can we still get a “why did judge pick A” explanation.

[15:21] Marissa Cole: We can store the judge rationale text, but that can still contain sensitive info. Alternative is store only a score and a categorical reason label, like “format better” or “more complete.”

[15:36] Miguel Alvarez: Score only is fine for gating.

[15:39] Marissa Cole: That’s consistent with what others asked too.

[15:43] Priya Raman: I want to ask about capacity again. We’re on dedicated. Would shadow run on the same cluster.

[15:51] Dylan Brooks: You have options. Easiest: same cluster but separate pool with a hard cap. Better: separate node group / replica set. We’ll recommend separate so shadow can’t starve primary.

[16:07] Priya Raman: And if we do separate, can you route shadow to a cheaper region.

[16:12] Dylan Brooks: Shadow can be region-scoped by policy, but if data residency matters, you’d keep it in-region. For US-only, you can keep it in US.

[16:22] Jordan Kim: We do have residency constraints for EU customers.

[16:25] Chloe Martin: Then you’d configure “shadow region = primary region” for those routes.

[16:31] Marissa Cole: Also you can set a per-region cap in the policy.

[16:35] Anika Shah: Okay. How do you prevent shadow from calling tools. Like if our prompt triggers a tool call, does that hit our tool endpoint.

[16:43] Dylan Brooks: Great catch. Shadow runs can be configured to either (a) disable tool execution and just evaluate the model output up to the tool call, or (b) replay tools against a sandbox / stub. Default is disable tool execution for safety.

[16:59] Miguel Alvarez: Nice. Because otherwise you’d be doubling side effects.

[17:03] Dylan Brooks: Exactly. Shadow must not cause side effects.

[17:07] Paula Mendes: In the UI it’s a toggle: “Allow tool execution in shadow: off.”

[17:13] Marissa Cole: Not in this mock yet, but yes.

[17:17] Anika Shah: For rollout gating, what are you recommending as “safe” metrics.

[17:22] Paula Mendes: Deterministic ones first: schema/format validity, safety policy pass-rate, and latency/cost deltas. Judge metrics are helpful but we recommend using them as “notify/hold” before “rollback,” at least initially.

[17:39] Miguel Alvarez: What about similarity metrics. Like embedding cosine between primary and shadow.

[17:44] Marissa Cole: We have a simple token-level overlap and optionally embedding similarity. But similarity is tricky; sometimes different is better.

[17:53] Miguel Alvarez: Exactly.

[17:55] Marissa Cole: So we show it, but we don’t recommend gating solely on similarity.

[18:01] Priya Raman: When a gate triggers, do you annotate the rollout timeline.

[18:06] Paula Mendes: Yes, the rollout view gets an event: “Shadow gate failed,” with the metric and threshold.

[18:13] Priya Raman: And alerting—does it page SRE or just notify in app.

[18:18] Dylan Brooks: Configurable. For shadow-only issues, default is warn, not page. For primary SLO issues, page. We don’t want shadow to cause noisy paging.

[18:31] Priya Raman: Thank you.

[18:33] Anika Shah: Can you show where quotas are visible to a user. Like how do we know we’re close to our cap.

[18:40] Marissa Cole: Yep. In Shadow Evals → Settings, there’s a “Quota & budget” panel. Shows daily tokens used, remaining, and projected burn.

[18:50] Miguel Alvarez: Is projected burn just linear.

[18:52] Marissa Cole: Right now yes, simple. Later we want it based on time-of-day patterns.

[18:58] Chloe Martin: Also there’s an API so you can pull it into your own dashboards.

[19:03] Jordan Kim: About access control, can we restrict who can enable shadowing.

[19:07] Chloe Martin: Yes, it’s a permission. Route policy write access plus a specific “shadow_evals:enable” permission. We can map it to your SSO groups.

[19:18] Jordan Kim: Okay.

[19:20] Miguel Alvarez: One more: does shadow run the exact same prompt including system messages, retrieval context, all that.

[19:27] Dylan Brooks: Yes, it mirrors the request payload as we receive it. If you do RAG externally and pass context in, that’s mirrored. If you do retrieval inside Redwood—some customers do—then it mirrors that too, unless retrieval would cause side effects. Typically retrieval is read-only.

[19:44] Miguel Alvarez: Okay.

[19:46] Anika Shah: For A/B tests, can we compare two shadow targets directly. Like not primary vs shadow, but shadow A vs shadow B.

[19:54] Marissa Cole: Not in MVP UI, but the data model supports it. Today we anchor everything to primary to avoid confusion. We can add “compare targets” view.

[20:07] Paula Mendes: From a policy perspective, gating is typically “candidate vs baseline,” which is primary. But yes, for exploration, A vs B is useful.

[20:17] Priya Raman: Any impact on logs. We already have a logging pipeline; we don’t want double.

[20:23] Chloe Martin: Shadow logs are separate and off by default. Metrics are on. If you enable sample logs, it’s a controlled sample rate with redaction.

[20:35] Jordan Kim: Good.

[20:37] Marissa Cole: I’m going to pause and see what else you want to dig into.

[20:41] Anika Shah: Can you talk about how this compares to just running offline evals. Like we do prompt sets in CI.

[20:48] Marissa Cole: Yeah. Offline is great for known scenarios, but shadow captures production-shaped traffic, prompt distribution, and tool usage patterns. It’s not ground truth, but it catches regressions that don’t appear in your curated set.

[21:05] Miguel Alvarez: That makes sense.

[21:07] Priya Raman: But it’s also scary because production traffic can be weird.

[21:11] Dylan Brooks: True, which is why we have strict kill switch, budgets, and “no side effects.”

[21:18] Jordan Kim: Competitor question: Bedrock has some eval tools. Why shouldn’t we use that.

[21:24] Marissa Cole: Bedrock’s eval is more offline / managed; it’s not integrated into your serving stack the same way. Our differentiation is it’s in the rollout workflow and it’s tied to the exact route config you’re changing, with the same runtime and same routing.

[21:41] Miguel Alvarez: Also Bedrock doesn’t cover our on-prem needs.

[21:44] Marissa Cole: Right.

[21:46] Anika Shah: Okay, so what’s beta timeline.

[21:49] Marissa Cole: We’re targeting limited beta starting end of November, early December for a few accounts. GA early next quarter if things go well.

[22:00] Priya Raman: Would we be in the first wave.

[22:03] Marissa Cole: Potentially yes, if we align on constraints—like sampling at 0.5% to start and one target.

[22:11] Miguel Alvarez: That’s fine.

[22:13] Anika Shah: What do you need from us.

[22:16] Marissa Cole: Mainly: pick one route, define what metrics you’d want to see, and what thresholds would make you stop a rollout. Also confirm your security posture around retention.

[22:28] Jordan Kim: We’ll want the retention doc.

[22:31] Chloe Martin: We can share our draft retention + redaction policy and the exact defaults.

[22:38] Priya Raman: And I want the specifics on alert thresholds so this doesn’t page us.

[22:44] Dylan Brooks: Yep. For beta we’ll set it so shadow failures are warnings unless they correlate with primary SLO changes.

[22:55] Miguel Alvarez: Can you explain “LLM-as-judge” a bit more. Like what prompt are you using.

[23:01] Marissa Cole: High level: we feed the judge the original user input (redacted if configured), the baseline output, and the candidate output, plus a rubric. The judge returns a preference and optionally category scores.

[23:15] Miguel Alvarez: Do you do pairwise with randomization so it’s not biased.

[23:19] Marissa Cole: Yes, we randomize A/B positions.

[23:23] Miguel Alvarez: Great.

[23:25] Priya Raman: Latency of judge itself—does that matter.

[23:29] Dylan Brooks: It’s in shadow pipeline. It can be slower. We cap it and time out. If judge times out, you get a “judge_timeout” count.

[23:41] Anika Shah: Okay.

[23:43] Marissa Cole: I’ll do a quick recap and then we can end early if you want.

[23:48] Marissa Cole: Recap: Shadow Evals lets you mirror sampled live requests to one or more shadow targets, run async, record quality and perf metrics, and optionally gate rollouts based on those metrics. You’ll have budgets (tokens/RPS), a bounded queue with drop behavior, and a kill switch. Retention/redaction is configurable, with defaults leaning minimal.

[24:12] Anika Shah: Sounds good.

[24:14] Marissa Cole: Next steps I captured: we’ll send the quota/budget semantics write-up, and the retention/redaction doc. You’ll send us your rollout gating preferences and pick one route for beta. Then we schedule a deeper dive with Priya and Jordan to go through SRE + security details.

[24:30] Priya Raman: Works.

[24:32] Jordan Kim: Yep.

[24:34] Miguel Alvarez: Thanks.

[24:36] Marissa Cole: Thanks all.

[24:39] (call continues with light scheduling / side chatter; transcript truncated)
